Chapter Three: Love, War, and the Search for Belonging.
Adulthood doesn’t always tiptoe in—it can rush at you all at once. Suddenly, there’s the thrill of new possibilities, but also the weight of real responsibility. The world outside was shifting fast, and when war broke out, it changed everything. For many, war meant heartbreak and upheaval. But, strangely enough, it also opened doors—creating space for growth and those moments when you discover what you’re really made of.
Work wasn’t just something to do; it was essential. Volunteering in a hospital dispensary—learning about medicines, even poisons—offered more than just a routine. It brought a sense of purpose and a treasure trove of knowledge that would come in handy later on. There was something special about falling into the rhythm of work, sharing laughter and challenges with colleagues, and feeling the quiet satisfaction of helping someone. Even in the darkest times, you realize—there are sparks of connection and meaning.
Then, love arrived. And with it, that mix of excitement and nervous uncertainty. The flutter of courtship, the heady rush of falling in love, and the tough but rewarding work of building a life together—each part of that journey shaped what came next. Marriage brought its own lessons: how to share, how to compromise, and how to hold each other up when things got rough.
The war years were tough—marked by separation, worry, and longing. But they were also a testament to human resilience. Letters became lifelines, tiny threads of hope to hold onto until reunion. Facing danger and loss left a permanent mark, but it also revealed strengths that had been hiding underneath all along.
Writing didn’t stop, even when time was scarce. Sometimes, it meant scribbling a few lines between shifts or after the kids were asleep. Those first successes didn’t come easy—they were earned through stubbornness and a willingness to learn from every misstep. But seeing that first story in print? Knowing someone out there was reading and enjoying it? That felt like its own kind of victory.
The longing for belonging—for a true sense of home—never really faded. The world felt huge and unpredictable, but family ties and the comfort of familiar places offered a kind of anchor. Turns out, home isn’t just somewhere you live. It’s that feeling of being truly known and loved.
Through all of it, taking time to reflect—looking back, making sense of everything—became a guiding habit. The lessons learned from love, loss, and resilience shaped not just stories, but a way of understanding life itself. Writing became more than just words on a page—it was a way to process, to heal, and to find meaning in the journey.
